description: Hash tables decomposed. The universal associative container. Hash function quality + collision resolution + load factor management determine performance. Three main collision resolution strategies: separate chaining, open addressing (linear probing, quadratic, double hash), Robin Hood / Hopscotch / Cuckoo. Resizing, hash flooding attacks, and cache-friendly layouts.

sub_mechanisms.name: separate_chaining
sub_mechanisms.definition: Each bucket holds a linked list (or small array) of entries. Collisions append to the bucket's chain. Lookup: hash → bucket → linear scan of chain.
sub_mechanisms.why: Simple to implement; load factor can exceed 1. Each lookup chases pointers (cache-unfriendly). Performance degrades gracefully with load factor.

sub_mechanisms.name: open_addressing
sub_mechanisms.definition: Single flat array of slots. On collision, probe to find an empty slot. Lookup probes until match or empty slot found.
sub_mechanisms.why: Better cache locality than chaining. Load factor capped at <1 (typically <0.7). Probing strategy matters — clustering can degrade performance.

sub_mechanisms.name: linear_probing
sub_mechanisms.definition: Open addressing where probe sequence is index, index+1, index+2, ... (mod m).
sub_mechanisms.why: Cache-friendly: sequential probes hit the same cache line. Suffers from primary clustering: long runs of occupied slots compound. Still the most common scheme in production (Rust HashMap, Google's SwissTable).

sub_mechanisms.name: quadratic_probing
sub_mechanisms.definition: Open addressing where probe sequence is index, index+1, index+4, index+9, ... (squared offsets).
sub_mechanisms.why: Mitigates primary clustering. But doesn't visit all slots unless table size is prime + load factor < 0.5. More complex than linear probing for marginal benefit.

sub_mechanisms.name: double_hashing
sub_mechanisms.definition: Open addressing with probe sequence: index, index + h₂(key), index + 2·h₂(key), ... where h₂ is a second hash function.
sub_mechanisms.why: Different keys have different probe sequences — eliminates clustering. Costs computing a second hash. Less cache-friendly than linear probing.

sub_mechanisms.name: robin_hood_hashing
sub_mechanisms.definition: Open addressing variant. On insert, if current slot's probe distance is shorter than the inserting key's, swap them.
sub_mechanisms.why: Reduces variance in probe distance — long probes get redistributed. Worst-case probe length is bounded. Used in Rust's HashMap (until SwissTable).

sub_mechanisms.name: cuckoo_hashing
sub_mechanisms.definition: Each key has two possible positions (via h₁, h₂). On collision, kick out the existing key + place it in its other position. Resize on cycle.
sub_mechanisms.why: O(1) worst-case lookup (check at most 2 positions). Inserts can cascade evictions. Memory-overhead trade for tight worst-case bound.

sub_mechanisms.name: swisstable_hashing
sub_mechanisms.definition: Google's SwissTable design. 64-byte cache-line-sized groups; per-slot 7-bit hash byte for SIMD scanning. Open addressing with quadratic probing.
sub_mechanisms.why: Modern cache-aware design. SIMD scans 16 slots per group in one instruction; 7-bit hashes filter false positives before full key comparison. Default in Abseil + Google's C++ codebase; adopted into Rust HashMap.

sub_mechanisms.name: tombstone_deletion
sub_mechanisms.definition: Open addressing's delete: mark slot as 'tombstone' (deleted, not empty) so probes can continue past it.
sub_mechanisms.why: Naively emptying a slot breaks probe chains: later searches would stop at the new empty slot, missing matches. Tombstones preserve the chain. Accumulating tombstones forces eventual rehash.

sub_mechanisms.name: resize_doubling
sub_mechanisms.definition: When load factor exceeds threshold, allocate a new table of double size + rehash all entries.
sub_mechanisms.why: Amortised O(1) per insert via doubling: total rehash cost is O(n) for n inserts. Rehashing is the expensive part — incremental resizing (Redis, Java) spreads the cost across operations.

sub_mechanisms.name: hash_flooding_attack
sub_mechanisms.definition: Adversary chooses keys that all hash to the same bucket, forcing O(n) per operation. The hash table degrades to a linked list.
sub_mechanisms.why: Real attack on web servers (POST a million colliding form fields). Mitigation: randomly-seeded hash function per process (Python's PYTHONHASHSEED, Java's String.hashCode randomisation), or use a hash function the attacker can't reverse.

derivation_rules.name: load_factor_controls_collision_rate
then: expected collision count grows roughly as α / (1 - α)
derivation_rules.why: At α = 0.5, expected probe is ~1.5; at α = 0.9, ~10. The non-linear growth motivates the typical 0.7 resize threshold — beyond that, performance degrades sharply.

derivation_rules.name: open_addressing_cache_friendlier_than_chaining
if: entries are in a flat array
derivation_rules.why: Pointer chasing (chaining) is latency-bound. Sequential array probing benefits from cache prefetching. Modern hash tables (SwissTable, Boost's flat_hash) use open addressing for this reason.

derivation_rules.name: good_hash_function_required_for_O1_expectation
derivation_rules.why: Uniform distribution means each bucket has expected O(1) entries. Bad hash (e.g., x mod 2 for even-mostly keys) concentrates entries — operations degrade to O(n). The hash function's quality IS the performance.

derivation_rules.name: salted_hash_prevents_flooding
if: hash function is seeded with per-process random salt
derivation_rules.why: Different processes get different hash mappings. Attacker-known collisions in one process don't apply to another. Mandatory for production-grade hash table implementations.

derivation_rules.name: resize_amortises_via_doubling
derivation_rules.why: Each entry copied O(log n) times across all resizes; total copies O(n log n / log n) = O(n) via geometric series. Per-insert amortised: O(1). Identical analysis as dynamic array doubling.
